children.html: explain how various features of Canada’s unique physical geography, including landscapes and landforms, can contribute to Canadian identity, and analyze the significance of the related symbols and images used in Canada and internationally

children.describer: By the end of this course, students will:
children.html: describe various characteristics of the natural environment and the spatial distribution of physical features in Canada, and analyze the role of physical processes, phenomena, and events in shaping them (FOCUS ON:Spatial Significance; Patterns and Trends)
children.title: Characteristics of Canada’s Natural Environment and the Impact of Physical Processes

children.html:
• the mountains in some regions of Canada are favourable for sports like skiing and snowboarding during the winter months
  • areas of the Canadian Shield in Ontario have an abundance of lakes and waterways, which attract tourism and support recreational use
  • within the Appalachian region in eastern Canada, diverse forests support the forest sector, and coastal areas support fisheries and small fishing communities
  • regions that were impacted by tectonic forces in the past may possess metallic minerals, which support mining and the development of mining-based communities
  • regions that were impacted by glacial activity in the past may possess aggregate resources that support employment in local communities
  • the physical characteristics of specific regions have shaped the cultures, knowledge, and ways of life of First Nations, Métis, and Inuit individuals and communities across Canada
children.label: Examples | Exemples

children.html:
• How do the physical characteristics of different regions in Canada influence tourism?
  • How could a graph showing seismic activity help land-use planners make decisions relating to urban settlement?
  • How would you use GIS to determine the best place to locate a wind farm?
  • How do soil, climate, and landscape influence agricultural practices (e.g., contour ploughing, ranching, livestock versus fruit and vegetable production)?
  • How is the impact of warmer temperatures on caribou migration affecting Inuit and First Nations communities in Canada’s North?
  • In which regions of Canada could you expect to have a career as a wheat farmer, logger, forestry technician, gold miner, greenhouse designer, rafting guide, member of the Coast Guard, coastal engineer, ship builder, cartographer?
children.label: Sample questions | Pistes de réflexion

children.html:
Students can:

  • use GIS to overlay maps of physical regions with layers showing transportation; population settlements; industries such as mining operations, forestry, and agriculture; and/or recreational activities, and can then use the maps as the basis for analyzing the interrelationships between the physical and human aspects of the regions
  • read satellite images or aerial photos to analyze relationships between the natural environment and human activities
children.label: Using spatial skills | Utilisation des compétences spatiales

children.html: analyze interrelationships between physical characteristics in specific regions of Canada and various human activities and communities that these characteristics support

• removing trees and paving over land can alter drainage patterns, cause sinkholes, and increase flooding in watercourses downstream 
  • some agricultural practices can contribute to soil erosion
  • removal of forest cover and vegetation for development can make slopes vulnerable to erosion and landslides
  • large-scale tree and vegetation removal can increase flooding, as roots are no longer present to absorb water and slow down water flow over the soil
  • damming of rivers for flood control, navigation, or electricity generation can submerge large areas, impact erosion and deposition of sediments downstream, increase the release of natural chemicals (e.g., heavy metals, gases), and disrupt the habitat, migration, and reproduction of aquatic species 
  • creating roads for forestry and seismic lines for mining can fragment habitat and disrupt migration and predator/prey relationships
  • restoring ecosystems can improve local air, soil, and water quality and improve biodiversity
children.label: Examples | Exemples

children.html:
• What are some of the environmental consequences of humans adapting the natural landscape to their needs (e.g., by building irrigation systems, clearing land, draining marshes)?
  • Consider a proposal for adapting a natural feature in your area for human use (e.g., filling in a wetland and building a shopping mall on the land). How might the proposal alter physical processes or affect natural events/phenomena in the area? How do the costs and benefits of this proposal compare with those of leaving the natural feature untouched or modifying it in a way that preserves most of its natural characteristics but allows some human use?
  • Why should land-use planners take into consideration local sensitive lands, such as wetlands, when developing new neighbourhoods?
  • How do megaprojects, such as the building of highways, influence drainage patterns and watersheds? How might these projects impact First Nations, Métis, and Inuit individuals and communities?
  • How does an increase in traffic into census metropolitan areas (CMAs) impact air quality in those CMAs in the summer?
  • How do the creation and use of winter roads impact the local regions in which they are located? What processes are impacted?
  • How might the development of new residential and commercial areas impact nearby forested areas, soil quality, and wildlife, now and for future generations?
  • How might blasting and drilling by some industries impact land stability and/or environmental sustainability?
children.label: Sample questions | Pistes de réflexion

children.html:
Students can:

  • use real-time GIS maps displaying air quality of a specific location over the course of a day to analyze the impact that local infrastructure and industry have on air quality
children.label: Using spatial skills | Utilisation des compétences spatiales

children.html: explain how human activities can alter physical processes and affect natural events and phenomena in Canada, including in their local region

Risks presented by physical processes and natural events:

  • high levels of precipitation in highland or upland areas may result in flooding of low-lying areas 
  • major seasonal variations in precipitation and temperature that occur in the continental climate expose communities in the boreal forest to the risk of wildfire  

Responses: 

  • ensuring that First Nations, Métis, and Inuit communities are consulted and involved in monitoring and responding to potential natural disaster risks in instances when they would be directly impacted
  • deploying Canadian military personnel to severely affected communities to aid in evacuation, relief distribution, and clean-up
  • facilitating the work of disaster and emergency relief organizations, including governmental, non-profit, and community organizations, to aid in disaster response and assist with relief efforts
  • making personal protective equipment available to vulnerable community members during wildfire season
  • building snow sheds over highways and rail lines in the Western Cordillera so that avalanches do not interrupt traffic or pose a risk to travellers
  • updating building codes in British Columbia to help ensure that recently built infrastructure is more resilient to earthquakes
  • incorporating Indigenous ecological knowledge (IEK) and practices in the monitoring of and responses to environmental changes related to potential natural events
children.label: Examples | Exemples

children.html:
• What criteria could be used to determine whether an event is classified as a natural disaster? How might that classification affect the response?
  • What are some ways in which municipal, provincial, and federal governments have responded to natural disasters? How would you assess the effectiveness of these responses?
  • What responsibilities do governments have to support communities in building their capacity to respond to natural disasters?
  • How does seasonal flooding in coastal regions impact some First Nations communities, including those along lakes and rivers? What practices have some First Nations communities developed to adapt or respond to these conditions?
  • What responsibilities do all levels of government in Canada have to protect communities from physical processes and events?
  • Why are disaster risks higher for some groups of people or communities, such as older Canadians, those with mobility issues, communities with insecure housing, coastal communities, Indigenous communities, or isolated communities?
children.label: Sample questions | Pistes de réflexion

children.html:
Students can:

  • use online maps or the Canadian Disaster Database geospatial views to assess hazard risks in relation to where people live in order to help identify the extent of the response needed in the event of a disaster
children.label: Using spatial skills | Utilisation des compétences spatiales

children.html: analyze the risks that various physical processes and natural events, including disasters, present to communities in Canada, and assess ways of responding to these risks

Consequences of changes:

  • warming in the North is leading to a shorter, less reliable ice season, less snow cover, and changes in plant and animal populations (environmental); threatening traditional Inuit culture (social); expanding opportunities for resource exploitation (economic); and creating conflict between countries over territorial claims (political)
  • melting of permafrost in Canada’s Arctic is leading to destabilization and shifting of buildings, including homes (social), and emissions of methane (environmental)
  • increasing frequency and duration of drought on the Prairies reduces agricultural production (economic), which leads to higher grocery costs (social), and also impacts the health of ecosystems and plant and animal populations in the area, making them more susceptible to the spread of invasive species, disease, and population decline (environmental)

Mitigation and adaptation strategies:

  • updating flood maps and local zoning by-laws to better prepare communities for the realities of flooding events made worse by climate change
  • creating public spaces with less concrete and more greenery, such as by using porous paving and implementing urban greenery projects, to facilitate the absorption of water into soil and to cool down urban areas
  • opening community cooling centres to serve unhoused people and those without air conditioning during heat warnings
  • completing a carbon emissions audit for a new public building project and taking action to offset the project’s carbon footprint and mitigate its impact on climate change
children.label: Examples | Exemples

children.html:
• What are the most significant social, economic, political, and environmental consequences of the increase in wildfires for various communities in Canada?
  • How did the Métis Nation of Alberta address issues around climate change and energy use when they built the Métis Crossing interpretive cultural centre?
  • How might the opening of the Northwest Passage affect Canada’s claim to Arctic sovereignty?
  • How can Indigenous ecological knowledge (IEK) about the land, water, and animals contribute to documenting the impacts of climate change in various parts of Canada?
  • How is habitat loss due to climate change impacting some First Nations, Métis, and Inuit communities that rely on certain species for sustenance and whose language, culture, and traditions are deeply connected to this relationship?
  • How is the federal government addressing climate change? How are some provinces and territories addressing climate change? What are some specific governmental strategies that impact your community?
  • How are some programs in Northern Canada integrating local Indigenous knowledges alongside data monitoring and satellite mapping to understand local ice conditions? Why would this be an important tool in addressing impacts of climate change?
children.label: Sample questions | Pistes de réflexion

children.html:
Students can:

  • use GIS or online databases and geospatial tools to plot the locations of past disasters and to make data-supported inferences as to why those disasters occurred in those locations
  • create an annotated map or spatial journal to show the impacts of climate change on different regions of Canada
children.label: Using spatial skills | Utilisation des compétences spatiales

children.html: analyze environmental, economic, social, and/or political consequences for Canada of changes in some of the Earth’s physical processes, including the impact of climate change, and assess local and regional mitigation and adaptation strategies

• the historical, economic, and cultural importance of natural places and landscapes to various communities, including First Nations, Métis, and Inuit communities
  • the cultural, traditional, religious, spiritual, or ceremonial significance of places or landforms
  • the cultural and spiritual connections that First Nations, Métis, and Inuit individuals and communities have with the land, including treaty and traditional territories
  • the interconnections between a community’s identity, the unique characteristics of its landscape, and the economy that forms around local natural resources
children.label: Examples | Exemples

children.html:
• What views do members of a local First Nation, Métis, or Inuit community hold regarding the use of the natural environment to meet human needs? How are these views similar to or different from those of an environmental organization? A multinational mining or forestry company? A local politician? The residents of a resource-based town?
  • How does Indigenous ecological knowledge (IEK) influence the beliefs of First Nations, Métis, and Inuit individuals and communities about the value of the natural environment? How have these knowledges influenced the way they have used and protected the land?
  • What is a current issue that highlights conflicting beliefs about the value of Canada’s natural environment and how it should be used or protected? What actions and processes are occurring in order to resolve the conflict?
  • What is the difference between a preservation and a conservation park system?
  • What are some reasons why various individuals and communities engage in the conservation and protection of various places, landscapes, and landforms?
  • How might the beliefs and values of individuals or groups shape public opinion about sustainability and stewardship?
  • How does the idea of wildlife protection relate to beliefs about the value of wildlife?
children.label: Sample questions | Pistes de réflexion

children.html: analyze how various communities value Canada’s natural environment, and how their practices and perspectives influence the use and protection of Canada’s natural environment

children.describer: By the end of this course, students will:
children.html: analyze interrelationships between physical processes, phenomena, and events and the ways in which various communities in Canada respond to and interact with them (FOCUS ON:Interrelationships; Geographic Perspective)
children.title: Interactions between the Natural Environment and Human Activities

children.describer: By the end of this course, students will:
children.title: Physical Geography and Physical Processes in Canada

children.html:
Characteristics of resources:

  • distribution
  • location/accessibility
  • abundance
  • sustainability
  • cost of developing
  • use/value
children.label: Examples | Exemples

children.html:
• What are some of the most abundant natural resources in Canada, and where are they located?
  • How does resource type (i.e., renewable, non-renewable, flow) affect the amount of a resource that is available for human use?
children.label: Sample questions | Pistes de réflexion

children.html:
Students can:

  • create maps to illustrate the locations of various natural resources, using appropriate symbols to indicate whether a resource is renewable or non-renewable, and how much of it is available in each location
  • use thematic maps on energy, forestry, geology and geosciences, mining and minerals, and water from the online Atlas of Canada and/or Ontario GeoHub to analyze the distribution of various resources
children.label: Using spatial skills | Utilisation des compétences spatiales

children.html: describe the characteristics of various renewable, non-renewable, and flow resources that are found in Canada

Natural resources’ relationship to physical geography:

  • oil and gas deposits are concentrated largely in the foothills of the Interior Plains 
  • critical minerals such as nickel, copper, silver, and cobalt are found in the Canadian Shield
  • potash is found in the Interior Plains 
  • forests supporting the forestry sector are found across Canada except in the Arctic and the southern Interior Plains
  • fish and other marine animals that are harvested for food are found in the oceans on Canada’s east, west, and north coasts
  • sand and gravel are abundant near past waterways and areas of glacial deposits
children.label: Examples | Exemples

children.html:
• How do the physical characteristics of a location, such as its landscape, geology, and climate, relate to the resources available there?
  • How do physical processes create or provide the conditions for a natural resource to be present at a particular location?
  • Where is most arable land located in Canada? Why? How might the distribution of arable land in Canada influence future land-use planning?
children.label: Sample questions | Pistes de réflexion

children.html:
Students can:

  • use GIS to examine photovoltaic potential or use solar resource maps to determine the best locations for solar farms in Canada
  • use GIS to determine some of the best locations for wind power generation based on wind patterns, weather, and proximity to energy markets
children.label: Using spatial skills | Utilisation des compétences spatiales

children.html: explain how the spatial distribution of key natural resources, including water, in Canada is related to the physical geography of the country

Interrelationships:

  • a region’s rock type determines which mineral resources are potentially available and the techniques used to extract and refine the minerals
  • a region’s topography, precipitation, temperature, and soil type determine the type of agriculture that is practised there
  • a region’s topography and hydrology determine the location of types of flow resources, such as wind and running/moving water, that can be used for electrical power generation
  • the method for harvesting trees is determined by the forest type and physical geography of their location

Innovative approaches:

  • research and development work being done by CanmetMINING on ways to break rock underground without the use of explosives
  • the development of wind turbine designs that are cold-weather friendly with de-icing and anti-icing mechanisms, which will allow turbines to continue operating efficiently under extreme conditions
  • Canada’s invention and use of CANDU heavy water nuclear reactors, which can use natural (i.e., non-enriched) uranium as a fuel – a technology adopted by numerous countries worldwide in the effort to produce energy more sustainably
  • the development of small modular reactors (SMRs), which are versatile and scalable and enable the building of nuclear infrastructure in a more cost-efficient way
  • research and innovation around Ontario’s critical minerals, such as chromite, cobalt, nickel, copper, and platinum, in relation to future low- and zero-emission vehicles
children.label: Examples | Exemples

children.html:
• What is the interrelationship between the availability of a resource and its economic value?
  • How might the presence of a resource in a relatively inaccessible location affect the cost and use of that resource?
  • How does the mode of extraction of drinking water from an underground aquifer differ from the extraction of drinking water from a lake? What are the costs and benefits of drinking water extraction from aquifers versus extraction from rivers and lakes?
  • What are some examples of technological innovations that improve resource extraction efficiency while mitigating ecological impacts?
children.label: Sample questions | Pistes de réflexion

children.html: analyze interrelationships between the location/accessibility and the mode of extraction/harvesting and use of various natural resources in Canada, including methods for clean energy production such as nuclear, wind, and solar, with reference to some innovative approaches to various modes of responsible resource development

Knowledge-based industries:

  • education, information technology, scientific research, journalism

Service industries:

  • banking, insurance, retail, health care, transportation

Cultural industries:

  • sports, the performing arts, film, radio
children.label: Examples | Exemples

children.html:
• What are some technological developments that knowledge-based industries in Canada are exploring or contributing to?
  • How might knowledge-based industries help develop new ways to support and improve resource-based industries?
  • What are some ways in which service industries help support the economy of a city, region, or province/territory? In what ways can cultural industries do so?
children.label: Sample questions | Pistes de réflexion

children.html: identify knowledge-based industries, and other industries based on human capital, and analyze their economic importance for Canada

Location factors:

  • availability and accessibility of resources/raw materials
  • transportation infrastructure and costs
  • energy/electricity infrastructure
  • communication networks
  • supply of labour with appropriate skill sets
  • market access/proximity
  • government policies and incentives
  • impact on local residential and First Nations, Métis, and/or Inuit communities
  • impact on local or sensitive ecosystems

Types of industries:

  • resource-extraction industries
  • manufacturing industries
  • service industries
  • knowledge-based industries
  • cultural industries

Interrelationship between factors:

  • a gold-processing plant may be located near a gold mine to reduce costly transportation of ore, but the location may require the development of energy and transportation infrastructure, and temporary housing and services for workers
  • Ontario’s ship-/boat-building industry is located in close proximity to the Great Lakes–St. Lawrence Seaway system and its many ports
  • the Holland Marsh is a successful agricultural area in southern Ontario, located on a drained wetland with rich soils, nearby water inputs for irrigation, and a temperate climate suitable for growing, with close access to transportation networks, a large market, and a large population of potential workers
  • southern Ontario has many auto assembly plants, which make use of the area's large population for both customers and workers, the close proximity to the American border, the dense transportation network to move materials in and finished products out, and government policies for attracting global automakers
children.label: Examples | Exemples

children.html:
• What differences do you see in the location of some major resource-extraction, manufacturing, and knowledge-based industries in Canada? What accounts for these differences? 
  • What are some resource-based communities in Canada? What accounts for their location? What are the implications for a resource-based community if the extraction/harvesting of its resource can no longer be sustained?
  • How can government policies affect decisions about where industries and economic activities are located?
  • What industries are dependent on certain levels of precipitation and temperature? What impact might changing climate conditions have on them?
  • What makes Sault Ste. Marie a suitable site for alternative energy development?
  • What, in order of importance, are the most significant location factors for an entertainment business?
  • Why would planners want to locate an industry that is dependent on raw material at the intersection of key transportation lines?
  • What factors contribute to Canso, Nova Scotia, being judged a good location for a new Canadian spaceport?
children.label: Sample questions | Pistes de réflexion

children.html:
Students can:

  • use existing data to map various industries and then overlay physical factors such as landforms, vegetation, and climate, and human factors such as transportation links (e.g., highways, railways, ports), energy infrastructure, and census metropolitan areas (CMAs), to identify correlations among the plotted factors
  • use a base map of Canadian towns and cities as well as maps showing a variety of key location factors to identify the best locations for businesses that they are interested in
children.label: Using spatial skills | Utilisation des compétences spatiales

children.html: analyze the interrelationship between the main factors that determine the location of sites for different types of industries in Canada

Importance of industries:

  • the service sector employs the vast majority of Canada’s population
  • Canada is one of the world’s largest exporters of minerals and agricultural products

International interconnections:

  • the role of international agri-food workers within Canada’s agricultural sector
  • the value of Canada’s natural resource sector in agreements, discussions, and political ties between Canada and other nations
  • the high level of Canada’s labour and environmental standards compared with those of other countries with similar export profiles (i.e., major natural resource exporters)
  • the amount and nature of Canada’s exports (e.g., natural resources, some manufactured products such as cars) and imports (e.g., manufactured products such as electronics, machinery, and automotive parts)
  • the impact of the Canada–United States–Mexico Agreement (CUSMA) on trade
  • the shared responsibility that Canada and the United States have for bodies of water such as the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence Seaway that are important for trade and transportation
children.label: Examples | Exemples

children.html:
• How does Canada’s physical geography support the production of clean energy and energy produced with zero emissions? How do the sources for our energy grid compare with those of other countries that Canada has economic ties with?
  • How does the availability of fresh water in Canada compare with the availability of fresh water elsewhere in the world? What are some industries that have developed around access to fresh water in Canada?
  • What are some of the more valuable resources found in Canada? Why are they valuable? Are these resources used in Canada or exported to other countries?
  • What Canadian resources do you predict that other countries will want to include in future trade agreements? Why?
  • Why are Canadian cultural industries important? How do these industries and the federal and provincial governments work together to protect/promote local cultural production?
children.label: Sample questions | Pistes de réflexion

children.html: assess the importance of different industries in the Canadian economy, and analyze interconnections between Canadian industries and those of other countries

• marine sector: navigator, marine pilot, hydrographic surveyor, marine environmental monitor, marine environmental economist
  • natural resource sector: risk assessment specialist, civil engineer or civil engineering technologist, geologist, logistics manager, forester, horticultural technician, park administrator or warden, conservation officer
  • tourism: tour director/operator, tourism marketer
children.label: Examples | Exemples

children.html:
• What benefit is there to a ship’s pilot or captain using geospatial technologies such as radar, GPS, and GIS while on the job?
  • Why is the ability to analyze radar and satellite imagery important for a meteorologist?
  • What spatial information might a forestry technician want to digitize and map using a GIS? How could this digital map be used by other workers within the natural resource sector?
  • Why would the ability to inspect, diagnose, and repair geospatial technologies on agricultural equipment such as tractors, combines, and sprayers be important for farmers?
children.label: Sample questions | Pistes de réflexion

children.html: identify some careers in Canadian industries, including the marine sector, the natural resource sector, and tourism, and explain how the use and application of geospatial technologies is an asset in these careers

Forms:

  • land that falls under historical and contemporary treaties
  • unceded land and lands subject to Indigenous title and other claims
  • privately owned land
  • public (Crown) land

Impact:

  • governments have a duty to consult and accommodate Indigenous communities when the proposed extraction of natural resources might affect them and their exercise of Aboriginal and treaty rights
  • settlement of land claims and historic grievances can contribute to greater certainty for economic development, including resource use and extraction, as well as support ongoing reconciliation between Indigenous and non-Indigenous peoples in Canada
children.label: Examples | Exemples

children.html:
• How might different elements of a resource management framework (e.g., national and/or provincial laws, international agreements, protocols of specific communities) attempt to address injustices faced by some First Nations, Métis, and/or Inuit communities? How successful have such frameworks been in this regard?
  • In what ways might the views of individuals and communities differ on the question of ownership of resources, such as water or air, that cross political borders?
  • Why was the inclusion of subsurface mineral rights in the Nunavut Land Claims Agreement Act important to Inuit communities? 
  • What is “unceded traditional territory” (also known as “Indigenous title lands”)? What are some of the implications, for government, industry, and Indigenous communities, of resource extraction on unceded traditional lands?
  • What role does legislation play in industry engagement with and inclusion of Indigenous people and their cultural practices in natural resource and other economic development? How effective is legislation in protecting Indigenous land rights?
children.label: Sample questions | Pistes de réflexion

children.html: explain forms of land tenure and ownership in Canada, including Indigenous land claims and land rights, andexamine the interplay between resource accessibility, extraction, and use in this country; Indigenous land rights; and economic reconciliation

children.describer: By the end of this course, students will:
children.html: analyze characteristics of natural resources and industries in Canada, and factors that affect the accessibility and use of natural resources and the location of industries (FOCUS ON:Spatial Significance; Interrelationships)
children.title: Natural Resources and Industries in Canada

children.html:
Models of and approaches to sustainable development:

  • the United Nations (UN) Sustainable Development Goals
  • the “three pillars” model
  • Circles of Sustainability
  • the Doughnut model
  • various Indigenous guidelines for sustainable development
children.label: Examples | Exemples

children.html:
• What is “sustainable development”? What are the UN Sustainable Development Goals? What assumptions were made in 2015, when these goals were created, that may no longer be relevant? How were Indigenous peoples from around the world involved in the process of creating these goals?
  • What actions are governments and non-governmental organizations taking to implement various sustainable development goals? How are community members, including youth, getting involved?
  • How are Indigenous peoples around the world working to protect threatened ecosystems?
  • What are some actions that governments in Canada and other countries are taking to protect ecosystems within the global commons? How are these governments working together?
children.label: Sample questions | Pistes de réflexion

children.html:
Students can:

  • use online tools, such as a demographic map or graphs found on a website, to track global progress towards some of the UN Sustainable Development Goals, and compare various countries to Canada in terms of their progress towards achieving the goals
children.label: Using spatial skills | Utilisation des compétences spatiales

children.html: analyze various innovative models of and approaches to sustainable development and how they are designed to foster a healthy environment, society, and economy

• economic, environmental, social, and political perspectives on the sustainable management of forest resources
  • economic, environmental, social, and political perspectives on the management of wild fish stocks
  • the competing perspectives and interests of municipal, provincial, federal, and First Nations, Métis, and Inuit governments in areas such as sustainable power generation, mining, or agriculture
children.label: Examples | Exemples

children.html:
• What are some of the impacts that the development of the rich mineral resources of northern Ontario’s Ring of Fire region have had or will have on Ontario’s economy? On First Nations communities in the area? On local economies in northern Ontario, including First Nations communities? How might these impacts affect the perspectives of various groups with a stake in this development?
  • What might a government need to consider in order to both grow the Canadian economy and protect the environment?
  • Why might different communities have different perspectives and interests related to what types of energy are available to residents and businesses? How might the needs of these different communities influence perspectives on the transition to net-zero-emissions energy production?
  • How does the forest sector take into account various values and perspectives in the development of sustainable forest management plans?
  • What are some careers related to resource development in Canada? How and why might these careers change in the future?
children.label: Sample questions | Pistes de réflexion

children.html:
Students can:

  • read various digital story maps on nature and biodiversity protection, such as ones on the Canadian boreal forest and bird populations, to analyze the relationship between forestry and biodiversity
  • use a GIS to analyze the impact of the development of resources in or near a First Nation community in Ontario
children.label: Using spatial skills | Utilisation des compétences spatiales

children.html: analyze issues related to the sustainable development of various resources and industries in Canada from a variety of perspectives

Strategies:

  • community composting and green waste collection
  • recycling and recovery programs
  • land protections
  • recovery of minerals from mine tailings
  • ecological restoration of aggregate quarries and mine sites
  • sustainable management of forests, fisheries, and wildlife
  • protecting and restoring natural areas
  • shifting industries to use of lower-carbon energy or clean electricity
  • tourism restrictions in environmentally sensitive regions
  • wildlife culling
children.label: Examples | Exemples

children.html:
• How effective are the waste-management practices in your community in supporting the sustainable use of consumer products? What happens to material that is recycled in your community? Is the recycling program reducing the amount of waste people produce?
  • How have various mine sites (e.g., open pit, quarry, and/or underground mines) been rehabilitated and reclaimed? How successful have these rehabilitation and reclamation projects been?
  • What societal impacts are associated with some renewable energy projects, such as the James Bay Project for hydroelectric power in Eeyou Istchee? How was Lac Seul First Nation impacted by the construction of a hydro dam?
children.label: Sample questions | Pistes de réflexion

children.html:
Students can:

  • analyze spatial data to evaluate strategies in Canada to protect the natural environment, such as government actions to protect land and water for the purpose of maintaining biodiversity
  • find and graph local data on the quantity of material being recycled compared to that going to landfill over time to assess the effectiveness of recycling strategies in different communities
children.label: Using spatial skills | Utilisation des compétences spatiales

children.html: describe strategies that industries and governments have implemented to increase the sustainability of Canada’s natural resources, and evaluate their effectiveness from a variety of perspectives

Governments, industries, advocacy groups, and local community organizations:

  • Ministry of Natural Resources and Forestry
  • First Nations, Métis, and/or Inuit organizations and communities
  • commissions and agencies
  • individual industries or industry associations
  • transnational corporations
  • trade unions and other labour organizations
  • non-profit and charitable organizations
  • engineering or environmental non-governmental organizations
children.label: Examples | Exemples

children.html:
• How have organizations and associations influenced how Canadian forests are used?
  • In what ways can the Niagara Escarpment be considered a natural resource? What are some groups that work on sustainability issues relating to the escarpment, and what are their concerns?
  • How do government subsidies influence the development and use of Canadian resources?
  • What impacts do different kinds of industries have on the environment, and how could they operate more sustainably? What are some examples of industries that are operated more sustainably in Canada than elsewhere?
  • How might innovation, entrepreneurship, and the UN Sustainable Development Goals support the sustainable development of resources and industries in Canada?
  • How are governments and industry leaders in Canada taking steps to help ensure access to affordable, reliable, and sustainable energy for all people living in Canada, including remote/isolated Indigenous communities?
  • How can community-held expertise, including that of First Nations and Métis individuals and communities, be used to inform the sustainable development and use of fish stocks in Ontario’s waterways?
  • How might a group of concerned residents influence government decisions about environmental protection or climate change policies?
children.label: Sample questions | Pistes de réflexion

children.html: analyze the influence of governments, industries, advocacy groups, local community organizations, and individuals on the sustainable development and use of selected natural resources in Canada

Issues:

  • in a globalized economy, the working conditions of those in communities around the world involved in extracting resources for and fabricating a product sold in Canada
  • the impact of fast fashion, with reference to the demand for natural resources and the disposal of used clothing, as well as advantages of the fast-fashion industry
  • shipping of recyclable materials, such as low-grade plastics and electronic waste, to other countries for processing
children.label: Examples | Exemples

children.html:
• What are some environmental, social, and economic impacts associated with the product you examined? What changes may occur in the future with respect to the availability of the natural resources required to create this product? What are some alternative methods of producing it that create a minimal impact on the environment?
  • How does the creation and consumption of this product affect the environment in Canada and globally?
  • Why might tapping into the second-hand economy help an individual improve the sustainability of their personal lifestyle? How does upcycling – bringing new life and value to goods that would otherwise have been disposed of – support innovation, creativity, and entrepreneurship? How can adopting the circular economy improve sustainability?
  • Why is it beneficial for a person to purchase goods that are labelled “Made in Canada”?
  • Which of the UN Sustainable Development Goals should be considered when evaluating the sustainability of everyday products?
  • How does a bottle/can-return program address issues related to the extraction of natural resources and the production, distribution, consumption, and disposal of products made from those resources?
children.label: Sample questions | Pistes de réflexion

children.html:
Students can:

  • create a map to trace the geographic reach of the life cycle of a product, from extraction of resources to disposal, and to explore the environmental footprint that results from transportation at all the stages of the product’s life cycle
children.label: Using spatial skills | Utilisation des compétences spatiales

children.html: analyze issues related to sustainability, with a focus on the resources extracted for, and the production, distribution, consumption, and disposal of, a few products that people living in Canada use in their everyday lives

children.describer: By the end of this course, students will:
children.html: analyze issues related to the sustainable development of resources and industries in Canada (FOCUS ON:Patterns and Trends; Geographic Perspective)
children.title: Sustainability and Economic Development

children.describer: By the end of this course, students will:
children.title: Managing Canada’s Resources and Industries

children.html:
Demographic characteristics and trends:

  • rate of natural increase
  • growth rate
  • age
  • sex at birth, gender distribution
  • cultural background
  • ethnocultural and religious diversity
  • percentage of population in urban areas
  • percentage of population in remote or isolated communities
  • population density
  • dependency ratio
children.label: Examples | Exemples

children.html:
• How is the percentage of working-age people (15–64) in the total population changing? What are the implications of this change?
  • What is the age distribution in your community? How does it affect your community now? How might the age distribution change in the future?
  • What factors might contribute to the demographics of the francophone population in various regions of Ontario? What is the growth rate of the francophone population in different regions of Canada?
children.label: Sample questions | Pistes de réflexion

children.html:
Students can:

  • analyze data from Statistics Canada graphs and maps and other sources to identify demographic patterns and trends within their own community, region, or province
  • develop their graphic communication skills by creating a variety of graphs to illustrate trends in and comparisons of statistics relating to demographics in Canada
  • analyze a series of population pyramids for different communities or areas to identify differences in age and gender structures of the various communities and how they have changed over time
children.label: Using spatial skills | Utilisation des compétences spatiales

children.html: analyze the major demographic characteristics of, and trends within, the population in Canada, and compare them to their community, local area, or province and/or to other communities, provinces, or territories

Quality-of-life/human-well-being indicators:

  • infant mortality rate
  • fertility rate
  • life expectancy at birth
  • birth rate, death rate, doubling time
  • access to medical care
  • access to clean water
  • literacy rate and access to education
  • labour force participation by industry
  • poverty rate
  • per capita income
children.label: Examples | Exemples

children.html:
• What is the Human Development Index (HDI)? What are its three dimensions? What indicators are associated with these dimensions? What are some patterns and trends related to these indicators across Canada? How do the patterns and trends differ for some specific demographic groups in Canada? Are there spatial variations in these patterns and trends?
  • What are some tools and methods other than the HDI that are used to measure quality of life?
  • In what ways does the poverty cycle contribute to infant mortality, life expectancy, and access to education?
  • How does access to education impact literacy rates, employment, and income?
children.label: Sample questions | Pistes de réflexion

children.html:
Students can:

  • use a scatter graph to identify correlations between two quality-of-life indicators
children.label: Using spatial skills | Utilisation des compétences spatiales

children.html: analyze interrelationships between factors that contribute to quality of life and human well-being in Canada, using a variety of skills, including data analysis

Migration trends:

  • changes in First Nations, Métis, and Inuit populations, including urban Indigenous populations
  • migration of workers to new locations to find jobs
  • migration of people from one province to another

Immigration trends:

  • increase or decrease in overall numbers
  • increase or decrease in the numbers in different immigrant categories
  • shifts in countries of origin
children.label: Examples | Exemples

children.html:
• Why might people leave a rural life and move to an urban area? Why might people move to another province or territory? What are the impacts of such migrations on society? On the community the people left? On the community they have moved to? On the people who are migrating?
  • In what ways are current migration and settlement patterns influenced by government policies?
  • What are some factors that contribute to the migration of Indigenous individuals and families to urban areas? How does this migration impact urban Indigenous communities? How does it impact their home communities?
  • How do race, income level, gender, and other social identity markers impact migration patterns?
  • What is the difference between a landed immigrant and a permanent resident?
  • What are the different categories in which immigrants can apply for entry into Canada? What factors affect the number of people applying in each category?
  • How does the total number of refugees in Canada compare to that in other countries around the world?
  • What issues or circumstances might make people want to leave their home countries (push factors)? Why might they choose Canada as their preferred destination (pull factors)?
  • In which regions of Canada are newcomers settling in the greatest numbers? What are the reasons for these choices? What types of incentives might companies and/or governments offer to encourage people to settle in a particular region, province, or territory?
  • How might immigration be used to help sustain growth of official languages in minority population situations, such as that experienced by francophones outside Quebec?
  • What trends are evident when you compare immigration and migration data for Ontario with those for another province in Canada?
children.label: Sample questions | Pistes de réflexion

children.html:
Students can:

  • use a GIS to create proportional arrows of varying sizes and thicknesses to illustrate population flows. Students can use these to analyze where migrants are coming from, where they are going, and how many people are included in each migration stream
  • compare quality-of-life indicators (e.g., infant mortality rate, literacy rate, gross domestic product per capita, percentage of population with access to potable water, number of doctors per 1,000 people) for Canada with those for other countries to help them understand why people might want to come to Canada
children.label: Using spatial skills | Utilisation des compétences spatiales

children.html: analyze trends in the migration of people within Canada and in immigration to Canada

Population settlement patterns:

  • scattered
  • linear
  • clustered

Population settlement types:

  • cities
  • towns
  • villages
  • hamlets
  • census metropolitan areas

Factors that impact size, distribution, and density:

  • landforms
  • climate
  • proximity to food and water sources
  • connections to transportation, communications, energy networks
  • economic networks
children.label: Examples | Exemples

children.html:
• Where do people live in Canada and why?
  • What are some physical factors that might influence the location of a settlement?
  • How might access to various forms of transportation influence the development and density of communities? How would a settlement pattern influenced by highway routes differ from one influenced by flight routes? By rail routes? By the location of waterways?
  • What are the advantages and disadvantages of living in a rural area, a suburb of a large city, or an urban area? Where would you prefer to live? Why?
  • In what ways can population patterns differ depending on the region or area, its histories, and/or its cultural contexts?
  • What pattern or patterns do you see in the location of First Nations communities in Ontario? Across Canada? What are some factors that account for the location of First Nations communities?
children.label: Sample questions | Pistes de réflexion

children.html:
Students can:

  • analyze data to identify correlations between population settlements and characteristics such as transportation routes, physical features, industries, and resources
  • create an annotated thematic map to highlight characteristics associated with different sizes of settlements across Canada. They can also use symbols of different sizes, based on various statistical intervals, to illustrate the relative size of different populations
children.label: Using spatial skills | Utilisation des compétences spatiales

children.html: describe patterns of population settlement in Canada, and assess the importance of various factors in determining population size, distribution, and density

• How do the population characteristics of your community compare with the population characteristics of two other communities in Canada?
  • How do the population characteristics of the three largest cities in Canada compare with each other? How might you account for the differences?
  • How do Canada’s general population characteristics compare with those of other countries around the world?
children.label: Sample questions | Pistes de réflexion

children.html: compare settlement and population characteristics of selected communities in Canada with those in other parts of the country and the world

children.describer: By the end of this course, students will:
children.html: analyze key patterns and trends in demographics and population movement and settlement, and factors that affect these patterns and trends, nationally and for various populations in Canada (FOCUS ON:Patterns and Trends; Interrelationships)
children.title: Demographic Patterns and Trends

children.html:
Effects of changes:

  • an aging population is increasing the demand for health care and institutional support, including housing for older adults
  • increased population density is affecting the need for housing, employment, and transportation, as well as access to green space
  • an increase in the number of working parents with responsibilities for both childcare and elder care places additional pressures on parents, increases the demand for daycare, and affects housing needs for some families
  • the growth of First Nations, Métis, Inuit, and urban Indigenous populations is increasing the need for education; housing; infrastructure; health care, including culturally appropriate health care supports; sustainable land and resource management plans; resolution of land claims and rights disputes; and cultural preservation and revitalization initiatives
  • increased diversity of newcomers is heightening the demand for language training and other support services
children.label: Examples | Exemples

children.html:
• What are some of the social, economic, and environmental challenges and opportunities associated with predicted increases in Canada’s population? What parts of Canada might experience the greatest impact from such increases?
  • What are some differences in the ways communities in Canada are being affected by the same major population trend or trends? What might account for the variations?
  • What are the impacts of the population growth rate of Indigenous peoples in Canada? What are some of the social, economic, and environmental impacts associated with the increased Indigenous population?
  • As Canada’s population ages, what changes will communities have to make to their infrastructure?
  • What future shifts might occur in Canada’s immigration needs? In Canada’s support given to refugees? What social, economic, or political impact might these changes have?
children.label: Sample questions | Pistes de réflexion

children.html:
Students can:

  • use statistical data to create graphs that illustrate changes in family structures over time
  • read graphs or thematic maps to analyze population trends over time
children.label: Using spatial skills | Utilisation des compétences spatiales

children.html: analyze current economic, social, cultural, political, and environmental effects that changes in Canada’s population are having on people living in various communities in Canada, and predict future impacts of these changes

• provision of health, cultural, and social support services in several languages
  • provision of language training and settlement services
  • development of businesses and social programs that enable seniors to continue to live at home and actively engage in their community
  • plans for greater services, including mass/public transportation, for rapidly growing areas
  • economic development initiative programs
children.label: Examples | Exemples

children.html:
• What are some federal, provincial, and municipal government programs that have been set up to accommodate newcomers and support their integration into the labour market? What criteria could you use to assess the success/effectiveness of these programs?
  • What kinds of non-governmental and/or community support services are available for newcomers? Who provides those services? How effective have those services been?
  • What are some school initiatives that are meant to address the needs of newcomers? How are these initiatives helping these students and their families?
  • What are some initiatives that French-speaking communities in Ontario and across Canada are taking to meet the needs of French-speaking newcomers? How are these initiatives helping newcomers settle in their new community?
  • What types of infrastructure and health care policies are needed to facilitate the continuity of care for Indigenous older adults within their home communities?  
  • What kinds of investments are being made to help meet the needs of older adults for personal medical assistance, home supports, social and community supports, and long-term care? How do these investments compare to the growing demand for these supports?
  • What can governments and employers do to help families balance work and childcare responsibilities?
children.label: Sample questions | Pistes de réflexion

children.html: evaluate various strategies used by governments and organizations to address the needs of Canada’s changing population

Opportunities:

  • cultural enrichment and intercultural exchange
  • new economic and trade opportunities related to globalization
  • increased awareness of global issues and injustices perpetrated abroad

Challenges:

  • increase in demand on social institutions, services, and municipal budgets
  • economic and social integration of newcomers
  • systemic discrimination
children.label: Examples | Exemples

children.html:
• In what ways can cultural diversity enrich the life of a community?
  • Why might tensions develop between people from diverse backgrounds? What individual, community, or government actions might prevent or reduce these tensions?
  • In what ways might an aging population provide opportunities for the development of specialized businesses, particularly in the service industry?
  • What difficulties might First Nations, Métis, and/or Inuit individuals encounter when they move from their home communities into an urban centre? What policies, programs, and community supports exist to help counteract these challenges?
  • What difficulties do newcomers to Canada encounter, and what policies, programs, and community supports exist to counteract these challenges?
children.label: Sample questions | Pistes de réflexion

children.html: describe ways in which population growth and demographic shifts within communities in Canada can create opportunities and challenges for individuals and groups within those communities

Global population issues:

  • food and/or water scarcity
  • environmental or political displacement
  • globalization facilitating the spread of diseases
  • inadequacy of health care and other necessary services
  • lack of, or restrictions on, education for girls
  • inequality of women
  • gender-based violence
  • urbanization and urban growth
  • climate change and its impact on communities
  • economic development in low-income countries
  • war and conflict

Roles and actions:

  • individuals: contributing to charities that provide relief and support to countries or communities in need; volunteering to assist with aid programs
  • non-governmental organizations: providing relief and supporting various types of projects in low-income countries; advocating for government policy changes
  • federal government: setting responsive immigration and refugee policies and practices; providing aid to low-income countries; contributing to the work of United Nations agencies
children.label: Examples | Exemples

children.html:
• In what ways has Canada’s spending on foreign aid changed over the past two decades?
  • Why should global disparities in health care be of concern to everyone?
  • What role does the World Health Organization (WHO) play in monitoring the spread of disease? What other intergovernmental or non-governmental organizations play a role in addressing issues related to health care? What types of aid do they provide?
  • What role does the Canadian military play in building international relationships and addressing global population issues?
  • How is Canada involved with the work of international organizations such as the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), the International Monetary Fund, and the World Bank? What role do those organizations play in global population issues?
  • What is the role of the Organisation internationale de la Francophonie (OIF)?  How do the member nations work together to address global issues?
children.label: Sample questions | Pistes de réflexion

children.html:
Students can:

  • use a cartogram, in which the size of land areas is proportional to the magnitude of the variable being mapped, to help them visualize global disparities with respect to such matters as access to food, water, health care, and education; vulnerability to disease; freedom from political unrest; consumption of resources; and carbon emissions
  • use scatter graphs to plot statistical data and identify correlations between various socio-economic indicators
children.label: Using spatial skills | Utilisation des compétences spatiales

children.html: identify global population issues that are of concern to people living in Canada, and analyze the roles of individuals, organizations, and governments in Canada, and the actions they take, in addressing those issues

children.describer: By the end of this course, students will:
children.html: analyze selected national and global population issues and their implications for Canada and for various people who live in Canada (FOCUS ON:Spatial Significance; Geographic Perspective)
children.title: Population Issues

children.describer: By the end of this course, students will:
children.title: Changing Populations

children.html:
Characteristics/distribution of:

  • transportation-related uses, including corridors, main arteries, residential streets, and public transportation routes
  • low- and high-density residential areas
  • industrial zones
  • commercial zones
  • parks, natural spaces, and other green spaces
  • recreational spaces and facilities
  • public/institutional land
  • agricultural land
  • central business districts
  • historic districts
  • trap lines
children.label: Examples | Exemples

children.html:
• Why might the location of a specific kind of land use within a community change over time? How might municipal layouts change over time with the introduction of newer planning and development ideas?
  • When analyzing the characteristics of residential areas, why is it important to consider affordability? What impact does a lack of affordable housing have on communities and the people who live in them?
  • Why is it important to build communities that are accessible for people with disabilities? How accessible is your community?
  • Why should the preservation of a variety of culturally significant sites, such as heritage buildings and landscapes, be considered in community planning?
  • What services does a community’s central business district or downtown provide? Why is a thriving central business district important to a community?
  • What benefits do public and recreational spaces and facilities provide for your community? Are all members of the community supported by the recreational spaces available?
  • Why is it important for land-use planners to be aware of diverse views, perspectives, and experiences and to consider these in the process of community planning?
children.label: Sample questions | Pistes de réflexion

children.html:
Students can:

  • read aerial photographs or satellite images of their community to identify different land uses and look for patterns. They can also use photographs to explore changes in land use over time and how they may have affected the local community
children.label: Using spatial skills | Utilisation des compétences spatiales

children.html: analyze the characteristics of different land uses in various communities in Canada, and explain how these characteristics and their spatial distribution affect those communities

Land use and land-use planning decisions influenced by nature:

  • limiting development in hazard-prone areas
  • improving infrastructure to help mitigate the impact of floods, wildfires, and rising sea levels
  • preserving and helping to rebuild and restore natural ecosystems that protect communities against climate-change-related hazards
children.label: Examples | Exemples

children.html:
• What are some ways in which the physical location of specific communities has influenced land use within them?
  • Why are many communities built on the shoreline of a body of water? What are the benefits of such a location? What are the risks?
  • Why is it important for land-use planners and developers to take into account the value of watersheds, wetlands, and prime agricultural land when making decisions about land use?
  • How are built landscapes being redesigned to accommodate more water from storm surges or high-precipitation events?
  • What role does green infrastructure play in supporting communities and their efforts to mitigate the impacts of climate change?
children.label: Sample questions | Pistes de réflexion

children.html:
Students can:

  • use topographic maps to analyze relationships between built features and physical features, and to predict possible impacts on both due to climate change
children.label: Using spatial skills | Utilisation des compétences spatiales

children.html: analyze the impact of the natural environment and physical processes, phenomena, and events, including climate change, on land use in the built environment as well as on land-use planning

• impact of the sharing economy on availability of housing/rental stock and affordable housing
  • impact of political decisions and economic shifts on the development of public transit and the expansion of highways
  • gentrification of urban neighbourhoods and its impact on housing affordability and on the people who have lived there
  • impact of increased development of large suburban chain retail stores on the business districts of local communities
children.label: Examples | Exemples

children.html:
• What impact have urban growth boundaries (UGBs) had on urban development?
  • How might infill projects that repurpose commercial or public buildings for residential development impact a community?
  • What barriers exist to creating affordable housing, and how can different levels of government assist in eliminating these barriers?
  • What is “youthification”? What is the interrelationship between youthification and gentrification in urban spaces? How has youthification influenced land-use planning and design?
  • What is meant by the term “cost of living”? What are some differences in the cost of living in cities across Canada? What are some ways in which the cost of living has affected people in various urban settings in Canada? What are some differences in the cost of living in isolated First Nations and Inuit communities compared to major urban areas?
  • What are some local, provincial, and federal government initiatives to help cities become more accessible?
children.label: Sample questions | Pistes de réflexion

children.html:
Students can:

  • create digital maps or analyze existing maps that highlight economic or cultural changes to an urban area over time
children.label: Using spatial skills | Utilisation des compétences spatiales

children.html: analyze some ways in which economic, social, cultural, and political forces affect various communities in Canada, including their land use and land-use planning

Impact of urban growth:

  • concentration of large quantities of waste in a limited area and risk of reaching the capacity of ecosystems to absorb them
  • urban sprawl leading to the loss of agricultural land and natural areas, including traditional land-use areas, along with species and ecosystems
  • environmental impact of increased energy consumption as a result of urban microclimates
  • impact of concrete, asphalt, and lawns on the environment and biodiversity

Strategies to control and/or mitigate the effects of urban sprawl:

  • construction of densely populated residential neighbourhoods
  • revitalization of older neighbourhoods
  • development of walkable communities
  • creation of protected areas and other natural spaces around and within cities
  • support for strategies to help modify the urban heat-island effect, such as installing cool and/or green roofs or painting roads and sidewalks with reflective white paint
  • creation of monitoring programs to assess water and air quality
children.label: Examples | Exemples

children.html:
• What do you think is the greatest challenge associated with urban sprawl? Why? What innovative initiatives are taking place in communities across Canada to address this challenge?
  • How does surrounding farmland support an urban community? What stresses might the community place on the farmland? How might the loss of nearby farmland affect a community?
  • How might the draining of a wetland for urban development affect drainage patterns, the microclimate, and/or plants and wildlife?
  • What impact might an increase in population density have on wastewater treatment processes and on nearby bodies of water?
  • What effects have increases in the amount of paved land had on groundwater? How have water bodies been affected by increased runoff from paved areas, and how might communities that use that water be affected?
  • What are some of the demands placed on infrastructure as urban areas continue to grow?
  • What are some ways in which various groups, including First Nations, Métis, and Inuit organizations, have collaborated with local governments in cities across Canada to ensure that urban development measures include consideration of environmental and cultural values? What were the outcomes of these initiatives?
  • How might land-use planners find a balance between competing values and interests in order to design and develop sustainable communities, given the limited space available for future development?
children.label: Sample questions | Pistes de réflexion

children.html:
Students can:

  • use official plans to assess the extent to which features such as protected lands, park areas, and bike lanes, which reduce the impact of urban sprawl on natural systems, have been incorporated into particular municipalities
  • use aerial images to analyze how much the area of a city has increased over time
  • use remote sensing images to analyze the increase or decrease of vegetation in urban locations
children.label: Using spatial skills | Utilisation des compétences spatiales

children.html: assess the impacts of urban sprawl, compact urban growth, and other types of urban growth on the natural and built environment, and analyze various strategies used to control urban sprawl and/or mitigate its effects

children.describer: By the end of this course, students will:
children.html: analyze characteristics and impacts of land use in various communities in Canada, including urban communities, and factors affecting land use and land-use planning (FOCUS ON:Spatial Significance; Patterns and Trends)
children.title: Land Use in Communities

children.html:
Issues:

  • the impact of shifts in food production due to climate change, competing land uses, pollution, and/or other environmental factors
  • food affordability and the impact of the increase in food deserts and food insecurity in some communities
  • loss of traditional trap lines and hunting territories
  • availability of country food for northern Inuit

Strategies:

  • improving soil conditions, restoring diversity in crops, researching innovative farming practices
  • supporting farmers’ markets or on-farm markets, the movement to buy local, and farm-to-table restaurants
  • consulting with First Nations, Métis, and Inuit leadership and Knowledge Keepers on methods for protecting traditional food sources
children.label: Examples | Exemples

children.html:
• What role does the availability of local food play in making communities more sustainable?
  • What are some examples of projects that support sustainable fisheries?
  • How might food businesses improve their sustainability practices? What role should the businesses involved with the production and/or distribution of food play in reducing the environmental impacts of food production, distribution, and consumption? In addressing the cost of food?
  • Why is food insecurity in Canada’s North a challenging problem to solve?
  • What is “food waste”? What are some innovative ways in which individuals and organizations are working to address it? How are online food-rescue platforms tackling the problem? What policies could be put in place to address food waste at the local and national levels?
children.label: Sample questions | Pistes de réflexion

children.html:
Students can:

  • use a GIS to map grocery stores in communities and identify food deserts in order to make recommendations on how to reduce the number of people who do not have easy access to food distribution centres
children.label: Using spatial skills | Utilisation des compétences spatiales

children.html: analyze issues related to the sustainability of Canada’s food system and strategies for managing and/or mitigating these issues

Options for development of transportation systems:

  • building new highways and/or widening existing ones
  • upgrading train corridors to increase capacity and/or speed
  • improving mass transit infrastructure and regional transportation networks between population centres
  • expanding bike lanes and rental bike/e-scooter networks
  • opening the Northwest Passage to seasonal passage for international shipping and tourism
  • expanding the use of electric passenger and vehicle ferries
  • improving charging-station infrastructure for electric vehicles along major transportation corridors, at hotels, and in centrally accessible locations in urban settings
  • expanding community-driven projects that respond to the need for accessible and reliable transportation for people living in and travelling between urban, rural, remote, and First Nations communities in Ontario
  • identifying and expanding green marine transport corridors for shipping
children.label: Examples | Exemples

children.html:
• How does urban growth contribute to traffic congestion in communities? What are some ways to reduce such congestion? What are some examples of traffic-reduction strategies from different parts of the world that could be applied in Canada?
  • Is high-speed rail a viable solution for traffic congestion in densely populated areas? Between major urban centres? How is high-speed rail used in other parts of the world and how might its use impact urban centres in Canada?
  • How do public transit systems benefit communities across Canada?
  • When you analyze access to public transportation in our community, what do you notice? What do you think would be the best options for future development? Why?
  • How might the establishment of more mixed-use neighbourhoods that provide a full range of services and employment, and that encourage biking and walking as the main methods of transportation, help address present and future transportation and development issues in urban areas?
  • Why might some transportation options be viable and effective solutions in some parts of Canada but not in others? What challenges do rural communities face in building or expanding public transit systems?
children.label: Sample questions | Pistes de réflexion

children.html:
Students can:

  • use various maps of their local community to identify locations and routes for possible sustainable transportation options
  • create a story map that highlights possible sustainable transportation options along an existing transportation corridor
children.label: Using spatial skills | Utilisation des compétences spatiales

children.html: analyze existing and proposed transportation systems, locally, provincially, nationally, and internationally, with a focus on their sustainability, and assess options for their future development

Policies and decisions:

  • government promotion of programs to make houses and industries more energy efficient
  • government policies on energy production in different parts of the country
  • corporate decisions to increase investment in renewable sources like solar, wind, hydro, and biomass
  • individual decisions to take public transit, ride a bicycle, or walk rather than to drive
children.label: Examples | Exemples

children.html:
• What are some ways in which governments in Canada promote and fund sustainable energy production? How effective are such policies in supporting the development of sustainable communities?
  • How might communities, including First Nations, Métis, and Inuit communities, meet the energy needs and wants of their residents with the least environmental impact? What role do governments, corporations, and individuals play in achieving this goal?
  • Which industries consume the greatest amount of energy? Is this level of energy consumption sustainable? What actions could these industries take to be more environmentally sustainable? 
  • What do we, as consumers, use the largest amounts of energy for? What are some ways in which we could reduce this use?
children.label: Sample questions | Pistes de réflexion

children.html: analyze the effects of government policies and corporate and individual decisions on energy consumption and production, and assess the implications of these policies/decisions for the sustainability of communities in Canada

Strategies:

  • improvement of community/neighbourhood amenities
  • support for local farmers’ markets and community gardening initiatives
  • preservation and expansion of green space
  • development and protection of naturalized parks with native species
  • investment in public services and infrastructure, such as transportation networks, health and social services, and recreational and cultural facilities
  • increase in educational opportunities
  • investment in diverse neighbourhoods
  • development of walkable communities
children.label: Examples | Exemples

children.html:
• What is the “multiplier effect”? How does the establishment or loss of a major industry affect other businesses in a community?
  • How have some towns that have lost their major industry been able to survive? Why have some other communities become ghost towns?
  • What kinds of public services and infrastructure does a community need to remain socially stable and economically viable?
  • What are some grassroots strategies for social and economic sustainability being implemented by First Nations, Métis, and Inuit communities?
  • How can the development of green spaces and innovative public spaces in urban areas help support social sustainability?
  • What strategies are some local community groups in Canada implementing to increase the economic or social sustainability of their communities? How are these different from the strategies implemented by governments?
  • What economic criteria would a plan for improving environmental sustainability have to meet in order to be practical to adopt and viable in the long term?
  • What is the role of environmental stewardship in supporting a sustainable community?

Students can:

  • use a GIS to analyze the walkability of a neighbourhood or community
